utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case. Yes, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-PT, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Status Conference under Rule 65 bis to look at the progress in the preparation of the case for trial. May I have the parties, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, counsel. For the Prosecution it would be Mr. David Re, trial attorney, Mr. Ronald Harris, trial support, and I Ekkehard Withopf, senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic and Stephane Bourgon from Montreal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Defence for Mr. Kubura. I am Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, attorney-at-law from Sarajevo, and Mr. Rodney Dixon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The first item is to inform the parties that the formal recording for the Rule 65 ter meeting which the parties had with the senior legal officer was not formally recorded as is the custom due to technical problems, so that the Tribunal does not have a formal record of this meeting at all. It is always the case that when these meetings are held, there is a formal record in the normal way, but something went wrong yesterday and we don't have a formal record. In this regard, the -- I would like to find out from the parties what matters they would like to place on record formally that were agreed to or decided upon or discussed yesterday, but not raising them as to be continued discussions during this Status Conference. It's just that it is important for the Trial Chamber to have any matters that were decided upon during that meeting which are important to the parties to be placed formally on record. I'll have the liberty to start with the Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an hour ago we were informed that we would not have this transcript, and we tried to prepare ourselves to inform you about the things that we wanted on record. The first issue that we discussed and that was agreed - and that should be on record - is the issue of disclosure of documents to help the Defence to be fully prepared for the trial. It was looked at from two points of view. One point of view was to what extent we already have judiciary decisions in other cases and to what extent we can have access to those. We now have the Appeals Chamber decision in the Blaskic case, but the list according to Rule 70 was received one day before the Status Conference, according to 65 ter. That's why we would like to inform the Trial Chamber that yesterday we filed a motion to the Trial Chamber in which we asked for the clarification of certain issues with regards to Rule 70. Likewise, we have not received the decision to access confidential material in the Kordic case. This is pending. We expect to have that very soon. But in view of the practice in the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case, we agreed during the 70 [as interpreted] ter conference that we would need after the decision -- we will need another month in order to access the confidential material in the Kordic case. We are -- as for the access to the confidential material, we are doing it again in the Ljubic case, in the Rajic case, and also in the Martinovic/Naletilic case, and we are going to file our motions these days. As for the access to the documents compiled by the European monitors, I believe that the situation is clear. We have encountered certain problems after a decision handed down by the Trial Chamber, and before this Status Conference we agreed the ways according to which this decision should be implemented. As for the issues of disclosure of documents on the part of the Prosecution, we agreed that the Prosecution has continued disclosing documents to the Defence. Yesterday, we submitted to the Prosecutor in keeping with the agreement that we reached at the meeting a new list of issues and questions for which we expect answers from the Prosecution. These questions are relative to the translation of documents according to the Rule 62(A), and also previous documents that we requested previously and have not yet been submitted. We also filed a motion for some documents to carry also the time of their issuance. The Prosecutor said that they might be able to submit the concept of the pre-trial brief to expedite the trial. We asked in our motion for this to be done in a -- within a reasonable deadline. We would also like to put on record that at the meeting we also discussed the decisions which are pending and that we expect. First and foremost, this concerns our request to confirm the right to appeal against the decision not to adopt our motion to put the case in abeyance. We were informed by the high judiciary council that the Trial Chamber, when it comes to the issues of jurisdiction and the amended indictment and other issues that we raised, that all these documents have been submitted to the Appeals Chamber, and I believe that our learned friends from the Prosecution will confirm that, once we were notified about that, we said that we agreed that if the Trial Chamber had reached such a decision, that both sides should have been informed about that. And the last issue that will be tackled by Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Dixon is the issues that were raised by the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic and General Kubura, and this is our request to apply the Rule 62 bis -- 62(A), and in keeping with the Rule 73, we will ask the Trial Chamber to reconsider their decision with regard to our written motion, the urgent written motion for the -- to hear the Defence counsel about the remuneration that they received for their work. We believe that this is an issue very important for this stage of the procedure. On the other hand, we believe that the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case, dated 24 May, gives us legal grounds to raise this issue before you. If it may please the Court, I will ask my colleague Bourgon to present legal justifications that we already presented in a meeting with the senior trial counsel. We did not wish to raise this issue at this Status Conference. We would like to inform you, Your Honour, about the reasons that we presented during the meeting. Since they were not put on record, we decided that we should raise the matter here during this Status Conference to have these reasons on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to be clear that what you are suggesting to do is to raise the matter so that the reasons can be on record and you are not raising an oral motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Firstly, we believe that this can be merged. During that session, we said that in keeping with the Rules, we will file an oral motion. However, we believe that presenting the oral motion and the arguments for that oral should be on record together with the requests and the arguments that we had already filed. In that way, we should be spared having to go over the same grounds twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. Before we go to the oral motion, you are finished with what you think the discussion was contained in the meeting yesterday, for purposes of having them on record?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not put forward the reasons that we wanted to raise together with our oral motion. They are now missing. We don't have them. But once you have heard them out, this will complement the meetings of the session according to the Rule 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Bourgon is going to put forth arguments concerning the oral motion for the Trial Chamber to reconsider their decision. This oral motion has been filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. As was indicated by my colleague, this is a motion for reconsideration of the Trial Chamber decision dated 17 June 2003, a decision of the Trial Chamber which denied our urgent motion for an oral hearing based on the allocation of resources to the Defence and the consequences thereof for the rights of the accused to a fair trial. In the same decision, the Trial Chamber denied our request for certification of the decision on the basis that the motion in itself was inadmissible because the Defence was not challenging the allocation of resources in its own case but, rather, was challenging the complete legal aid system before the Tribunal. This motion will be divided into two parts. I will take care of the first part, which includes, first of all, the test applicable for reconsideration of Trial Chamber decision, as well as the first leg of this test, dealing with new facts. My colleague, Mr. Rodney Dixon, representing the accused Kubura, will take care of the second part of this motion, dealing with the erroneous character of the decision and the resulting prejudice to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving into the first part of this motion, the applicable test to allow a Trial Chamber to reconsider its decision. I referred the Trial Chamber to a decision rendered by the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case, case number IT-95-14-A, for appeals. The decision is entitled as follows: "Decision on Prosecution's preliminary response and motion for clarification regarding the decision on joint motion of Hadzihasanovic, Alagic, and Kubura of 24 January 2003." In this decision from the Appeals Chamber, the test to determine whether a Trial Chamber should and can reconsider its own decision is laid out at paragraph 7. I will read from this decision: "The Appeals Chamber also observes that in some of the submissions made in the motion for clarification reconsideration of the decision is what is actually sought by the Prosecution. In this regard, the Appeals Chamber recalls that a Chamber may reconsider a decision and not only when there has been a change of circumstances where the Chamber has been persuaded that its previous decision was erroneous and has caused prejudice." End of quote from paragraph 7 of the Blaskic decision of the Appeals Chamber. Also referring in a footnote 13 to a decision Prosecutor versus Zdravko Mucic et al., case number IT-96-21-A bis, judgement on sentence appeal dated 8 of April, 2003, Appeals Chamber. It is our submission, Your Honour, that this is the test to determine whether this Trial Chamber can and should reconsider its decision. The test is twofold: Has there been a change in circumstances - the part that I will be arguing - and was the decision erroneous and has it caused a prejudice - the second part, which will be argued by Mr. Dixon. With respect to the change and circumstances, it is our submission this afternoon, Your Honour, that there has been two changes in circumstances. The first one is our request to the President to get involved further to the Trial Chamber's decision. As mentioned earlier, the Trial Chamber's decision was filed or was rendered on the 17th of June. Further to this decision, we have highlighted what our arguments would be during the 65 ter Conference on the 30th of June and we have filed a -- we have sent a letter to the President which explains the complete background to this Defence team, as well as the Defence team of Mr. Kubura -- of the accused Kubura, to obtain additional resources to prepare the case for the Defence during pre-trial. The letter was sent to His Excellency Judge Meron, President of the Tribunal, on Monday, the 7th of July. Further to this letter which was sent to the President, we have been informed today that the President considers it inappropriate to get involved because it is a matter for the Registry to take care of and because the Trial Chamber is already seized of the matter and has denied our request for certification. This is a change of circumstance because it now deprives us of any other alternatives but to returning before the Trial Chamber to get a result on this issue. The second part of the change of circumstances is the fact that, further to the Trial Chamber's decision, the Defence of both the accused Hadzihasanovic and the accused Kubura have entered into discussions with the help of the Dutch Bar Association and its president, have entered into discussions with a firm - an independent firm - to come and evaluate and assess the work that would be reasonably required for -- in any Defence team to prepare the case for the Defence in this case. It is our submission, Your Honour, that the biggest problem with respect to the situation we face, with respect to allocation of resources, is that no one has accepted to look and to sit down with us and to go through exactly the work that we have done so far and to say whether this work was reasonable and necessary and, if not, to tell us; and, if so, to evaluate how many hours of work are required to prepare the case for the Defence based on the information we have provided to the Registry. For this reason, we are -- we are of the belief that the work or an evaluation performed by an independent and external agency to the Tribunal will be able to highlight the fact that the resources allocated so far to the Defence are insufficient, and insufficient way beyond what we have received so far, and that it also has created a prejudice, as will be highlighted later by Mr. Rodney Dixon. For us to proceed with an evaluation will be a costly exercise. We have met with the Registry, and we have explained to the Registry what we are about to do and why. In our view, we should not have to pay for such a study, and there would be other ways to handle this matter. However, now, because we have no other avenues to pursue to get a result and to get an answer to our problem, we will be hiring this firm. We are in contact at the present time with two different firms. Both are international law firms. One is from London and the other one is from Germany. One of the two, we hope, will accept our mandate, which is double-pronged, and that is the answer to the first question is: The work we have done so far, was it reasonable and necessary to prepare the case Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for the Defence? And question number two: How much work? What is the quantity of hours required by the Defence to prepare a case of this magnitude? In all likelihood, we hope to be able to produce such a report by mid-August at the latest, at which time this report will be forwarded to the Trial Chamber as an addendum to the present oral motion, indicating a change of circumstances and a reason for a Trial Chamber to intervene and reconsider its decision, because this, the differences in the resources we have been allocated and the resources that we need to prepare the case for the Defence, there is a big difference between the two, which creates a fair-trial issue for which a Trial Chamber needs to intervene. I will now hand over to Mr. Dixon for the second part of this motion. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you sit down, Mr. Bourgon, on this move you are making to consult one -- the two firms that you have mentioned, who will pay for their services?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At the present time, Your Honour, we will most likely have to borrow money to pay for this evaluation. I can inform the Trial Chamber that this study will cost 15.000 Euros. It will be a six-day exercise. The firm will -- we will have, of course, to enter into discussions with the Registry, and we will have also to inform the Trial Chamber of the identity of the firm in order to ensure confidentiality of the documents that they will have access to. They will have access to all documents that we have in our files, both the documents that have been given to us by the Prosecution and any documents we may have obtained in investigating the case for the Defence. They will then have access to our offices in Sarajevo, to our offices here in The Hague, and we will have then -- the way this is structured so far: We will have private interviews, the four counsel, with this firm to answer any questions they may have as to why we may have filed a particular motion or why we may have done -- taken certain action in this case. This is the -- basically the outline or the mandate given to this firm. The result, as I've mentioned, will be produced to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And so in view of the fact that you did say you had filed this motion and you are now putting your reasons on record, the Trial Chamber would have to wait for this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As I've mentioned, Your Honour, we feel there are two parts to this test. We feel that the second part of the test, the fact that the decision in our view has an erroneous character in law, it would be sufficient for a Trial Chamber to intervene at this stage without waiting for this report. Should the Trial Chamber wish to wait for the report and to go on both aspects of the test for reconsideration, then of course we will be -- we will gladly file this report with the Trial Chamber at the earliest opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. So I will hear the second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If I may --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Regarding the report and payment for the report, the Registry has been formally requested to provide funding for the obtaining of such a report, as is relevant to this case and can be relevant to future cases as well, and could well be an important independent study to be used in the future. But the only indication is that the Tribunal would not be prepared to fund such an exercise. Hence, as Mr. Bourgon outlined, other initiatives have been taken to provide the funding. Your Honour, on the second leg, taking it swiftly with regard to the erroneous nature of the Trial Chamber's decision, it is our submission, Your Honour, with respect that the decision was erroneous in three respects. Firstly, the decision of the Trial Chamber did not consider that the main issue put forward by the Defence, that being whether or not the refusal to provide further funding to the Defence impacts upon the ability to have a fair trial for the accused. That is clearly a matter within the purview of the Trial Chamber. And the decision does not address whether or not a fair trial can be undertaken, given the limitations on Defence funding. It has been our submission that it clearly does impact on the continuance of a fair trial because we are hampered in our ability to prepare the Defence for trial and also that has to be cost against the continuing work that the Prosecution is undertaking in investigating the case and preparing it for trial. No blame is being cost on my learned friends from the Prosecution in this regard. They have to fulfil the obligations. But so does the Defence in order to prepare for trial. And therein lies the prejudice to the accused. It's a matter of ensuring that all necessary preparations are undertaken, revising the extensive documentation in the case, interviewing witnesses, both Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses, considering the pre-trial brief that the Prosecution will prepare, and whether admissions can be made in order to shorten the proceedings, to prepare the Defence's own pre-trial brief, and to do the nitty-gritty trial preparation before the trial commences. Clearly the two or three months before the trial commences have to be taken up with intensive work in preparing, in particular, cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses that have been identified, and also with the Prosecution attempting to narrow the issues, and hence, to shorten the trial. Without funding to do that, it makes the task of the Defence counsel extremely difficult and that directly impacts upon whether or not the defendant can receive a fair trial both in preparation but also if that -- it will help you in the trial when matters simply might not have been covered which should have been covered. The second area, with respect in our submission, is that the Trial Chamber identified the correct test to be applied in the circumstances as one of whether the Registrar has acted unreasonably or not, and found that the Registrar hadn't done so. Our first submission in that regard is that, as I indicated from the outset, the correct approach would have been to look at it from whether or not it impacts upon a fair trial. But secondly, even if it is considered from the point of view of whether the Registrar acted reasonably, it's our submission that he could not have done so in the circumstances. And we say that on the basis of the calculations which we have done and put before the Trial Chamber regarding the number of documents alone which we have had to consider in the case. These are documents disclosed by the Prosecution, clearly documents that have to be considered - other related documents - and our own documents from investigations where we have discovered archived material. And we have calculated, based on the work that's been done, based also on the Registry's guideline, which is that it takes two minutes to review a document - this is an official policy of the Registry, which might be conservative, but nevertheless we have used that as our guideline - that it would take us at least 4.500 hours - that's counsel hours - to review the documents. That is not reviewing them from the outset and reviewing every document. It's looking at documents that have been narrowed down by investigators and reviewing them specifically for the purposes of preparing for trial. That doesn't include the hours that are required for motions, pre-trial briefs, the intensive preparation that I've referred to already. The Registrar says that 3.000 hours is sufficient. We say 4.500 hours is a minimum simply to look at the documents. In our submission, that is a -- a vast gulf that lies between the two, and it can only lead to one conclusion: If our calculations are correct, which we say they are, then the Registrar has acted unreasonably in assessing the number of hours that are required. The Trial Chamber's decision did not address whether or not our calculations were accurate, whether or not they were reasonable, and as a result whether further hours should be ordered. Hence, another ground, the second ground, as to why the decision was erroneous, in our submission. Instead, what the decision did was to focus on whether or not the Defence were challenging the entire system or looking at only the circumstances in their case, coming to the conclusion that the entire system was being changed, which is not a matter within the jurisdiction of the Trial Chamber, and hence the motion was ruled inadmissible. Our submission is that that - and this is the third reason why the decision was erroneous - was wrong, on the basis that our submissions from the outset have always been focussed on our particular case and the circumstances involved in our case. We have never submitted that the entire system should be changed. We've focussed on what was required to meet our needs and our needs alone, without referring to -- to other cases. And we've specifically set out the exceptions which arise in our case as to why the 3.000-hour limit should be extended. The policy of the Registrar recognises that that limit might need to be extended but only in exceptional circumstances. Our argument is that those circumstances have arisen, and yet the decision of the Trial Chamber does not consider them or indicate whether they have not arisen. Taking it very briefly, Your Honour, the main exceptional circumstances are - and these have been outlined in a number of our documents - firstly, the excessive length of time that it has taken for us to obtain access to confidential documents. We are still waiting that in the Blaskic and Kordic cases. Some 23 months have passed in this regard, and that could never have been foreseen. That time should have set aside to deal with matters that are still outstanding at this very late stage. In addition, new cases have arisen that could not have been foreseen at the time. For example, the case considering the accused Rajic, which is directly related to our case, concerning the Vares area. And there we've had to now set in motion an application to obtain access to the material in that case. Clearly more time is going to be required to look at all of that material. In addition, thirdly, there have been amendments to the indictment. Your Honour will be well aware of these. And there's no need to rehearse the entire history once again. But in particular, concerning the international armed-conflict issue, jurisdictional questions have arisen which have absorbed substantial amounts of time, which could not have been foreseen, given the changes the Prosecution made and yet again made late in the day. There's also been an application for other amendments to the indictment, in respect of my client, Mr. Kubura, if those amendments were granted, it would in effect mean that he's charged with - in my submission - for four additional murders. Those are substantial allegations, as Your Honour will appreciate, which have to be investigated, requiring further time. Those are some of the main exceptional circumstances that -- that have arisen, requiring us to request further hours. We say that that can be done within the existing policy of the Registrar, which allows 3.000 hours, but in exceptional cases further hours to be granted. It's not a challenge to the whole system, hence the decision of the Trial Chamber with respect was erroneous in this regard. And, Your Honour, lastly, an additional point which we -- we do wish to place before you, Your Honour, is whether or not it was correct in the first place for this matter to be referred to the Trial Chamber. We accept that the directive does allow the Registry to consult the Trial Chamber on the matter, that is Article 22(A) of the directive. But it's our submission that that article applies to situations when, at the outset of a case the Trial Chamber has been involved in determining with all the parties the length of the pre-trial period and what lump-sum payment would be appropriate. That didn't occur in this case, and hence it was not appropriate for the matter to come to the Trial Chamber when it had not been involved in the first place. It should have been sent, according to the scheme that allowed - and this was the previous scheme under the directive - the matter to be sent to the President. So that is a matter which we also wish to place on record as a -- a legal problem with the way in which this matter has been conducted. The next effect, Your Honour, is that the accused are prejudiced. The Prosecution can continue to function without the same, continues to investigate the matters, continues to make disclosure to us in various areas, and we are at a stage where we are yet to see the Prosecution pre-trial brief. We are yet to have a finalised indictment. There is much work on the road ahead before we get to trial. And without further resources - even if it be a limited amount, to cover our basic office expenses and costs - it would be extremely difficult to provide the defendants with the necessary assistance in preparing their defence. The equality-of-arms principle, in our submission, is seriously in jeopardy unless this matter is reviewed. It's for all those reasons, Your Honour, that we request the decision of the Trial Chamber be reconsidered. On this leg alone, it would not be necessary to wait for any further report. There are new facts in the report, when that come, but on this leg alone we submit that our application can be considered forthwith by the Trial Chamber. Your, those are the submissions on Defence on this matter. And if there's anything further, it has to be raised by my colleagues. I think Mr. Bourgon does wish to raise one further matter, Your Honour. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I -- quickly to conclude on our oral motion presented before you this afternoon. We'd like to bring the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that the decision was rendered yesterday by Trial Chamber III in the case of the Prosecutor versus Ojdanic. Without going into the details of this decision, there are basically two issues which are highlighted by Trial Chamber III in its decision. The first one appears to be mismanagement of resources, and the second issue appears to be that counsel had accepted the fact that there was a cap on the number of hours they would receive to prepare this case at pre-trial. With both of these issues in mind, it is our submission this afternoon that both of these do not apply to our team. First, we never were asked to -- we were never asked to accept or to consent to any specific cap on the resources allocated to us. As a matter of fact, for the record, it is important to note that from the outset this case was initially ranked at level 1, in accordance with the policy of the Registry. Thereafter, the case was then ranked to level 2 and then further upgraded to level 3. All along we have always said to the Registrar that whether or not we would reach level 3, this would be insufficient, based on our estimation of the work required to prepare this case. I simply conclude this motion by the relief requested from the Trial Chamber in reconsidering its decision, which will be one of two things: We would hope that the Trial Chamber by reconsidering its decision would order the Registry to allocate further resources for us to be able to prepare the case for the Defence and to make this a fair trial. The second possibility of the relief that we would request from the Trial Chamber is at a minimum to obtain the Registry to fund this independent study or to appoint someone who will be able to look at the work we have done and to evaluate the work we have done and to openly tell us, if that is the case, where we went wrong, and where we did too much work. And if not, then to allocate further resources to us. Respectfully submitted, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We'll go back -- oh, maybe I should ask the Prosecution if they have any matters they would like to raise on the oral motion as stated by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. There are only very few issues the Prosecution wants to raise. First of all, the Prosecution acknowledges the immense magnitude of this case being a pure 7(3) case and having 25 crime-based incidents involved. The Prosecution also acknowledges the right of the accused for a fair trial and also acknowledges the equality of arms principle. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The Prosecution will, however, not take a position in respect to the motion for two reasons: Number one, in the past, these proceedings have been ex parte proceedings. The Prosecution is not in possession of the materials that the Registrar and the Trial Chamber has been provided with in the past; and number two, and that's the main reason, that's a policy reason, as a matter of principle the Prosecution will not get involved in such issues in the context of remuneration of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall move on to other matters in this Status Conference. First of all, I should ask the Prosecution whether they do agree on the matters that were agreed and discussed in the meeting for purposes of them being formally on record, before we move to pending motions and disclosures and other things. Maybe there are other matters which the Prosecution can remember which they would like to put formally on record as having been discussed during the Rule 65 ter meeting with the senior legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The issues that have been discussed during that meeting have been correctly summarised by my learned colleague Mrs. Residovic. There are only three issues, three matters the Prosecution wishes to add: First of all, the Defence again appreciated that the Prosecution is in compliance with its disclosure obligations. The disclosure is ongoing on a very regular basis. The second issue is the ECMM issue. There was a discussion on this issue. My learned colleague, Mrs. Residovic said there was an agreement, however a partial agreement. However, I do understand that this issue will be a matter for further discussion in the course of this Status Conference. And finally, the issue of the pre-trial brief. It is correct that the Prosecution announced that provided the Appeals Chamber decision will not be rendered in the very near future and a scheduling order for the filings of the pre-trial briefs will not be rendered in the very near future, the Prosecution will provide the Defence with a draft of the pre-trial brief within a reasonable time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the draft of the pre-trial brief will be -- will depend on the -- will be based on the current indictment, as it stands, on which we are waiting for the Appeals Chamber decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The draft of the -- of the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution will be based on the indictment which has been proposed to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll move on in our Status Conference to the matters that are still pending. The Trial Chamber is dealing with the joint Defence request for certification regarding the decision on motion for leave to amend the amended indictment dated 18th June 2003, which was filed on 26th June 2003. As for the other motions which are pending before the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber will be in a position to deal with them as soon as the Appeals Chamber decision has been rendered, which hopefully will be before the summer recess. On matters of disclosure, I think, from the report that has been submitted, matters seem to be moving between the parties. And from the report, I don't see any problems regarding that, unless somebody or some party wishes to discuss that. Disclosure seems to be moving very well. I don't see anybody raising an issue. The Trial Chamber has been receiving regularly the reports on the compliance of the accused persons with the conditions on provisional release and that is satisfactorily up to date. There are no unusual circumstances that can raise any matters regarding the continuation of the provisional release. So the provisional release will continue on the same conditions as before. Regarding the archives with the EUMM matter which the parties have been discussing, the Trial Chamber have been informed that the Prosecution is proceeding with asking for consent under Rule 73 so that if the consent is granted, then disclosure can forthwith proceed to the Defence. That is the position. Can I have confirmation from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution is in contact with EUMM in Sarajevo. I actually contacted them today. Unfortunately, none of the persons who would be able to make decisions were available. I was told the relevant people will be available tomorrow. I will first contact them verbally to get a first insight in their position. Once this is done, a formal request will be sent to EUMM in Sarajevo to lift the restrictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure the Defence will be following the progress on that with the Prosecution, and we will wait to see what result the Prosecution will get. And perhaps only after that, maybe other matters - depending on whether or not the consent is given - maybe at that stage some other matters may be raised by the Defence if they so wish. Is there any comment on that from the parties? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are grateful to the Prosecution for investing an extra effort in implementing the decision of this Trial Chamber. We would, however, like to confirm that any further problems that might possibly arise can only be resolved if we can rely on the decision of the Trial Chamber. We believe that this decision is the basis upon which the Prosecution and the Defence will attempt to resolve all pending issues with respect to access to the archives. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The only other matter that is on the schedule is to discuss the probable date for commencement of trial in this case, in view of all the matters that are pending and the fact that there are other cases which are about to be ready for trial soon after the recess and the availability of a Trial Chamber to take this case on trial is being considered. But looking at the progress in the other cases, which are more or less ready for trial, I'm able to say that this case would -- there would be a Trial Chamber ready to take up this case on trial during the month of November, so the Trial Chamber expects that once the major hurdle that we have - and that is the Appeals Chamber decision - is rendered, then everything else will move smoothly, because we have been looking at the motions that are pending all this time while waiting for the decision of the Appeals Chamber. And thereafter, the parties will move. I think the stages that are remaining will be fulfilled within the month of -- the rest of September and October so as to make it possible for the trial to start, because this is one of the cases that have been pending in pre-trial for some time now, and the Trial Chamber would like to see the trial start. From the report on the meeting that was held with the parties with the senior legal officer, there is quite a -- the Prosecution have reached quite an advanced stage, in terms of their lists which are required to be served on the Defence under Rule 65 ter. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The list for the statements of witnesses and the actual witnesses and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. The Prosecution identified the majority of its witnesses, obviously, and also identified the majority of its documents that will follow part of the exhibit list. However, as already indicated in the course of the last 65 ter Conference, in particular in respect to the documents, additional documents will certainly be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Is there any other matter that the parties would like raise? None. The Prosecution? None. Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber will consider the oral motion on the fees raised by -- as raised by the Defence as soon as possible so that the matter can be decided, and perhaps we can move on in this case. There being no other matters to be dealt with during this Status, the Status Conference is closed and the Court will rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
